name: Consistent sleep schedule

lead: Going to bed and waking at the same times each day is basic sleep-hygiene advice and costs nothing.
Sleep research links poor or irregular sleep with metabolic and hormonal changes, but no study tests the practice for appearance.

paras: It is proposed to keep the body clock and hormone rhythms aligned.
No risks are documented. Sleep hygiene alone is not supported as a stand-alone insomnia treatment by a 2021 meta-analysis.

forums.title: Consistent Sleep Schedule: The Ultimate Free Improvement Tool for Hormones, Height & Puberty Gains

lead: A consistent sleep schedule means going to bed and waking at about the same times every day, including weekends. It is a standard element of sleep-hygiene advice and is discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a free way to support hormones, growth and recovery.

Reference sources state that a regular wake time tends to improve sleep, though overall evidence that sleep hygiene alone treats insomnia is weak.[1] Research links irregular sleep patterns and poor sleep quality with obesity-related measures in adolescents[2] and sleep disorders with hormonal and metabolic changes,[3] but these are associational findings and none addresses appearance directly.

paras: The practice fixes bedtime and wake time within a narrow window. Sleep-hygiene guidance recommends waking at about the same time each morning.[1] The term "hygiene of sleep" dates to Willard Moyer in 1903, and Peter Hauri's 1977 book brought behavioural sleep rules into modern sleep medicine.[1]

A study of adolescents with overweight and obesity associated sleep duration, quality and bedtime shift between weekdays and weekends with obesity severity and weight-related behaviours.[2] A 2025 review described how sleep disorders affect hormone secretion, glucose tolerance and inflammation.[3] A shift-worker review discussed interventions for sleep management.[4]

No studies found testing a fixed bedtime for appearance outcomes. A randomized trial of a sleep health education programme and a personalised sleep app among 1,355 employees examined sleep and productivity outcomes,[5] and a 2021 meta-analysis cited in reference sources did not support sleep hygiene alone as an insomnia treatment.[1]

Forum posts present a fixed bedtime during puberty as a free tool for growth hormone, testosterone, height and skin. One thread claims up to 15 percent larger growth hormone pulses with a fixed 8.5-10 hour sleep window.[6] The sources reviewed do not show a trial testing this claim.

lore.intro: Forum threads describe a fixed bedtime as a free "maxx" for hormones and height, particularly during puberty.[6]

claims.claim: A fixed 8.5-10 hour bedtime boosts growth hormone and testosterone, including up to 15 percent larger GH pulses.

timeline.event: Peter Hauri publishes No More Sleepless Nights.[1]
